claims.text: A transient liquid-phase sintering agent melting between 800 and 900 °C will facilitate rapid densification of an Mg-transition-metal powder blend.
Liquid-mediated diffusion will suppress elemental segregation in an Mg-Zr-Ti-type alloy.
The proposed process will produce a metastable single-phase solid solution on cooling without forming brittle intermetallics.
Mg-transition-metal powders have inherent instability from Mg volatility and tend to form segregated, multiphase microstructures during conventional solid-state sintering.
A Mg-rich eutectic or transition-metal hydride can act as a transient agent that forms a liquid at approximately 850 °C.
A rapid cycle at 900 °C with a 10–15 minute hold and quenching is the proposed processing route.
Vacuum or inert argon will prevent Mg oxidation during processing.
A heating rate above 50 °C/min will minimize Mg evaporation before formation of the liquid phase.
A transient liquid phase enhances atomic diffusion by orders of magnitude relative to solid-state diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion will homogenize the Mg-transition-metal mixture and dissolve incipient segregated phases before solidification.
The transient liquid lowers the activation energy for diffusion and thereby bypasses kinetic pathways leading to segregation and multiphase formation.
Rapid quenching prevents re-precipitation of brittle intermetallics, analogous to the reported cooling response of HfNbTaTiZr.
A short dwell time minimizes Mg loss by evaporation.
The process will yield greater than 95% theoretical density while retaining a mass density below 6 g/cm³.
The resulting material will have a homogeneous, single-phase-like BCC or FCC microstructure with substantially reduced elemental segregation.
Removing segregated phases will improve oxidation and corrosion resistance by eliminating galvanic couples.
Standard solid-state sintering of Mg-transition-metal powders at 800–1000 °C produces less than 90% relative density, significant Mg loss, and segregated intermetallic phases.
Above 1000 °C, rapid Mg evaporation causes porosity and failure of the density target.
Below 800 °C, the single-phase target fails, while excessively long dwell times allow nucleation and growth of segregated intermetallics.
The CrMoNbWV study provides an example of Laves-phase formation at the lower end of its investigated sintering-temperature range.
